assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped trade theory after the Krugman-style models. They changed how trade is analysed, with consequences for productivity, welfare and policy, and they opened a large empirical literature on exporters. The framework is now the standard foundation of the field.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution on selection and the gains from trade. Helpman contributed to the broader heterogeneous-firm and trade-structure agenda, including work on firm-level trade and on matching and wages. Redding is important for quantitative and spatial extensions, but those are more derivative of the core insight, so I would limit the prize to two people.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation, with extensive empirical support and many applications. It is mature enough for recognition now.
uncertainties: Other trade-theory contributors, such as Bernard, Jensen and Eaton-Kortum, may also be argued to belong to the credit.
Whether the committee prefers to honour Helpman for the Grossman-Helpman political-economy work instead.
My view of the relative credit shares comes from general knowledge and has not been verified against the literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit-cycle amplification provide a core mechanism linking financial frictions to aggregate fluctuations. The mechanism was made newly central by the 2008 crisis and is widely used in macro-finance and policy models.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is the clear theoretical landmark on collateral and credit cycles. Gertler's work, including the financial accelerator papers with Bernanke and Gilchrist and the later intermediary models, extends it. Bernanke's earlier Nobel in 2022 may affect how the committee weighs the financial accelerator strand.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of influence, extensively applied and tested after the global financial crisis. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Gertler's credit overlaps with the New Keynesian and financial-accelerator strands, and the relationship to the 2022 prize may be an issue.
Direct empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Modern political economics integrates electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal outcomes into formal and empirical analysis. It created a coherent research programme with broad consequences for understanding institutions and policy.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini developed the theory and cross-country evidence on constitutions and electoral rules. Besley contributed on state capacity, accountability and development politics. The group is coherent, though the committee could consider narrowing it.
assessment.maturity: Developed since the 1990s, with a substantial cumulative empirical record. Mature.
uncertainties: Cross-country identification of constitutional effects is contested.
The closely related institutions literature, honoured in 2024, may affect how the committee judges novelty.
Possible committee-member relationships with Persson, which are disclosed but not adjudicated here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance transformed how economists think about legal institutions, investor protection and financial development. It also inspired a large body of comparative-institutions research in corporate finance and development. The empirical conclusions remain debated, but the agenda-setting effect is large.
assessment.attribution: The core papers are the La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny series. Shleifer is also central to behavioural finance and other fields, which complicates how credit should be allocated. Vishny is a co-author on the foundational papers, so omitting him is a defensible but contestable choice given the three-laureate limit.
assessment.maturity: Foundational work from the late 1990s, with extensive follow-up and critique, which gives a strong basis for a balanced assessment.
uncertainties: Legal-origins identification has been seriously criticised, and later work has revised some conclusions.
The three-person limit forces a choice among four co-authors.
Non-prize considerations about individuals are outside this assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data brought new measurement of mobility, neighbourhood effects and the long-run effects of childhood environments. The research has had strong policy influence and set new empirical standards in public economics.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the agenda. Hendren is central to the neighbourhood-effects and causal place-effects work. Katz is credited through the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis and earlier work. Friedman is an important co-author, so the three-person limit forces a difficult choice.
assessment.maturity: Mostly work from the 2010s onward. It is influential, but the long-run replication and policy-experiment evidence is still accumulating.
uncertainties: Relatively recent timing compared with other candidates.
Credit allocation across a large team of co-authors.
Whether measured place effects are causal in all settings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework is the main workhorse for monetary policy analysis in central banks. It combines nominal rigidities with microfounded dynamics and rules. Its practical and academic impact is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is widely dispersed: Calvo on staggered pricing, Taylor on rules, Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans on medium-scale DSGE and Smets on its estimation. Woodford, Gali and Gertler represent the synthesis and policy analysis. Any three-person selection leaves out obvious contributors.
assessment.maturity: Developed over three decades and a basis for policy. Mature, although it was tested by the post-pandemic inflation and heterogeneous-agent critiques.
uncertainties: Diffuse attribution makes a three-person prize difficult.
Earlier prizes to Lucas, Sargent, Kydland-Prescott and Phelps overlap with parts of the agenda.
Gertler's overlap with B043.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence changed understanding of labour-demand change, wage inequality and the local costs of trade adjustment. The work influenced both research and policy debates.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the common thread through the task approach and the trade-shock papers. Hanson and Dorn are central to the China-shock work. Acemoglu, Katz, Levy and Murnane are also important to the task framework, and some of this credit overlaps with other prize discussions.
assessment.maturity: Main papers from 2003 and 2013 onward, with ongoing replication and reassessment. It is reasonably mature but not fully settled.
uncertainties: Some trade-shock findings have been questioned on persistence and mechanisms.
The task-framework credit extends beyond this ballot's named group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification provides a principled way to report what data can reveal under weak assumptions. It changed methodological thinking in econometrics and is applied in policy analysis and structural work, so its significance goes beyond one field.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the founder of the approach, including the bounds literature. Tamer contributed key work on inference and moment inequalities. Molinari is an important developer of the inference methods, and the three-person limit leaves her as a close alternative.
assessment.maturity: Manski's foundations date from the late 1980s and 1990s, and the inference theory matured over the following two decades. The field is established, though practitioner adoption has been slower than for design-based methods.
uncertainties: Practical adoption and influence on mainstream applied work are less than for competing methodology candidates.
Credit allocation between Manski and the inference developers.
Econometrics was recognised in 2021, which may affect committee appetite for another methods prize soon.
